variants.title: Run the caption path
variants.context: A captioning request crosses five boundaries: decode and route the image, encode visual tokens, generate bounded candidates, ground every claim against evidence, then release or abstain under route policy. Generation proposes language; the release path decides what may leave the system.
variants.prompt: A screen reader requests alternative text for an uploaded photograph. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Apply route, accessibility, and safety gates, then return a caption, a review state, or no caption.
Encode patches, layout, and OCR into visual tokens while preserving the evidence identifiers.
Validate the media, apply orientation, hash the image, and select the accessibility route policy.
Link each noun, attribute, action, and quoted string to visual, OCR, or approved context evidence.
Decode bounded caption candidates under the token, latency, and repetition budget.

variants.hint: Which stage is allowed to decide that a fluent sentence may not ship?
variants.explanation: Evidence identifiers must survive encoding so the grounding stage can link claims back to regions before the product gate runs.

variants.title: Run the caption path
variants.context: A captioning request crosses five boundaries: decode and route the image, encode visual tokens, generate bounded candidates, ground every claim against evidence, then release or abstain under route policy. Generation proposes language; the release path decides what may leave the system.
variants.prompt: The upload is a screenshot of a quarterly revenue chart and the candidate caption quotes a printed figure. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Decode a candidate that states the quarterly revenue figure in words.
Extract layout and OCR so axis labels and the printed total keep their spans.
Return the identification plus a long description, or hold the caption for review.
Route the validated screenshot to the complex-image path instead of the general photograph path.
Compare the quoted figure with its OCR span rather than with the decoder score.

variants.hint: A quoted number is a claim like any other.
variants.explanation: Quoted text is grounded against the OCR span it came from, because a high decoder score is not evidence that the characters were read correctly.

variants.title: Run the caption path
variants.context: A captioning request crosses five boundaries: decode and route the image, encode visual tokens, generate bounded candidates, ground every claim against evidence, then release or abstain under route policy. Generation proposes language; the release path decides what may leave the system.
variants.prompt: The grounding service is unavailable while a search-metadata request is in flight. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Encode the image and request claim evidence from the grounding service.
Fail closed for automatic release and return an explicit pending state to the product.
Record that the grounding dependency returned no evidence for the candidate claims.
Accept the upload, hash it, and select the search-metadata route.
Decode a fluent candidate while the evidence request is still outstanding.

variants.hint: What happens when a required release dependency is missing?
variants.explanation: When a required grounding or policy dependency is unavailable the system fails closed for automatic release and shows a pending, review, or unavailable state.

variants.title: Stage the release
variants.context: Release gates are pre-committed: qualify on frozen offline evidence, observe in shadow without returning candidate captions, canary inside an approved blast radius, then expand or roll back the model and policy bundle together.
variants.prompt: A new caption model and its policy bundle are ready for production. Put the release stages in order.

items.text: Run production-shaped traffic in shadow without returning any candidate caption to a user.
Expand exposure only while every hard gate stays healthy.
Assign stable cohorts to a route canary inside the pre-approved blast radius.
Pass data lineage, hallucination, accessibility, safety, slice, and latency tests on the frozen offline sets.

variants.hint: Which stage is the first one a user can feel?
variants.explanation: Each stage buys different evidence, and exposure grows only after the cheaper stage has already been passed.

variants.title: Stage the release
variants.context: Release gates are pre-committed: qualify on frozen offline evidence, observe in shadow without returning candidate captions, canary inside an approved blast radius, then expand or roll back the model and policy bundle together.
variants.prompt: During the canary, unsupported object claims rise sharply on the low-light slice. Put the events in order, ending with the correct response.

items.text: The canary cohort exposes a hallucination regression on the low-light slice.
Offline frozen sets pass every declared gate.
Shadow traffic shows no disagreement large enough to stop the rollout.
The model and policy bundle is rolled back together rather than partially.

variants.hint: The bundle that shipped is the bundle that reverses.
variants.explanation: Rollback reverses the whole model and policy bundle, because a caption decision can only be reproduced when its versions move together.

variants.title: Stage the release
variants.context: Release gates are pre-committed: qualify on frozen offline evidence, observe in shadow without returning candidate captions, canary inside an approved blast radius, then expand or roll back the model and policy bundle together.
variants.prompt: Shadow traffic runs, but stage latency for the OCR path is not being recorded. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Restore the missing telemetry so a canary verdict can be explained and reproduced.
Only then assign canary cohorts inside the approved blast radius.
Run shadow traffic and discover that OCR stage latency is missing from telemetry.
Qualify the candidate bundle on the frozen offline sets.

variants.hint: One hard gate is about the evidence itself, not the captions.
variants.explanation: Decision telemetry complete enough to explain and reproduce an outcome is a hard gate, so a canary that cannot be explained should not start.

variants.title: Budget the decode path
variants.context: The decoding lab models a request as encoder time plus the decoder base cost plus a per-beam cost for every beam beyond the first. Greedy decoding keeps one path, so its effective beam width is always one.
variants.prompt: A rainy bus stop scene encodes in 42 ms. Grounded reranking costs 31 ms of decoder base work plus 10 ms for every beam beyond the first, and the route runs at beam width 4. What is the modeled request latency?
variants.hint: Only the beams after the first one carry the per-beam charge.
variants.explanation: Modeled latency is encoder time plus decoder base cost plus the per-beam cost of the extra beams, so 42 plus 31 plus 30 is 103 ms.

mistakes.feedback: Charged the per-beam cost for all four beams instead of the three beyond the first.
Left out the per-beam cost of the wider search entirely.

variants.title: Budget the decode path
variants.context: The decoding lab models a request as encoder time plus the decoder base cost plus a per-beam cost for every beam beyond the first. Greedy decoding keeps one path, so its effective beam width is always one.
variants.prompt: A quarterly chart encodes in 58 ms. Language-only beam search costs 24 ms of decoder base work plus 8 ms per beam beyond the first, and the route runs at beam width 3. What is the modeled request latency?
variants.hint: Count the extra beams, not the total beams.
variants.explanation: 58 plus 24 plus two extra beams at 8 ms each is 98 ms, and the higher encoder cost of a dense chart is paid before any decoding starts.

mistakes.feedback: Charged all three beams instead of the two beyond the first.
Dropped the per-beam search cost from the estimate.

variants.title: Budget the decode path
variants.context: The decoding lab models a request as encoder time plus the decoder base cost plus a per-beam cost for every beam beyond the first. Greedy decoding keeps one path, so its effective beam width is always one.
variants.prompt: A meeting room scene encodes in 46 ms. An operator requests beam width 4 but the route is configured for greedy decoding, whose decoder base cost is 18 ms and whose per-beam cost is 0 ms. What is the modeled request latency?
variants.hint: What effective beam width does greedy decoding actually run?
variants.explanation: Greedy decoding keeps one path, so the requested width is ignored and the estimate is 46 plus 18, or 64 ms.

mistakes.feedback: Applied a per-beam charge even though greedy decoding keeps a single path.
Used the grounded reranking base cost of 31 ms instead of the greedy base cost.

variants.title: Choose the decoding policy
variants.context: Decoding searches language, not truth. Greedy is fast and deterministic, beam search compares several partial sequences and can favor generic fluent priors, and sampling adds variety but needs stronger grounding and reproducibility controls.
variants.prompt: An on-device accessibility route must answer inside a strict deadline and must return the same caption for the same image on every retry. Which decoding policy fits?
options: Nucleus sampling, because varied wording helps screen reader users.
Beam search at width 8, because more candidates raise caption quality.
Greedy decoding, because it is fast and deterministic for a fixed input.
optionFeedback: Sampling makes retries disagree with each other, which is the opposite of what this route needs.
A wide beam multiplies decoder work and still gives no reproducibility guarantee.
Correct: one path per step is the cheapest option and reproduces the same caption every time.
variants.hint: Which property does the route need first, variety or repeatability?
variants.explanation: Greedy decoding is deterministic and cheap, which is what a deadline-bound reproducible route requires; grounding still runs afterwards.

variants.title: Choose the decoding policy
variants.context: Decoding searches language, not truth. Greedy is fast and deterministic, beam search compares several partial sequences and can favor generic fluent priors, and sampling adds variety but needs stronger grounding and reproducibility controls.
variants.prompt: An editorial tool wants to offer an author three genuinely different draft captions per image. What should the route do?
options: Sample several candidates and ground each one before showing it.
Return the greedy caption three times with different punctuation.
Raise the length penalty until the single caption gets longer.
optionFeedback: Correct: sampling supplies variety, and every shown candidate still needs claim evidence.
Repunctuating one caption gives the author no real alternative to choose between.
A longer caption is not a second option, and extra detail raises hallucination risk.
variants.hint: Variety is a decoding property; support is not.
variants.explanation: Sampling can supply editorial variety, but each candidate is still a proposal that must pass claim grounding before an author sees it.

variants.title: Choose the decoding policy
variants.context: Decoding searches language, not truth. Greedy is fast and deterministic, beam search compares several partial sequences and can favor generic fluent priors, and sampling adds variety but needs stronger grounding and reproducibility controls.
variants.prompt: The candidate with the highest language score names a bus that no evidence supports. What should the system change?
options: Keep a reranking or filtering stage that can reject the top-scoring candidate.
Tune the length penalty until the bus phrase becomes less likely.
Trust the cross-attention map over the bus region as supporting evidence.
optionFeedback: Correct: candidate generation must be followed by a stage with authority to reject a fluent sentence.
Penalties reshape wording without ever checking whether a claim has visual support.
Attention weight shows where the decoder looked, not that the object is present.
variants.hint: Which stage is allowed to say no to a high-scoring sentence?
variants.explanation: Language scores rank wording, so grounded reranking or filtering must be able to reject a high-scoring candidate outright.

variants.title: Route by image function
variants.context: W3C guidance makes the text alternative depend on the image's purpose. Informative images convey the essential content, decorative images take empty alternative text, functional images describe the action, and complex images need a short identification plus equivalent structured information.
variants.prompt: A page contains four images. Match each one to the alternative text behavior its function requires.

pairs.label: Informative news photograph
pairs.detail: Convey concisely the essential information the surrounding content depends on.

pairs.label: Decorative section divider
pairs.detail: Use empty alternative text so screen reader navigation is not padded with noise.

pairs.label: Magnifier icon inside the search button
pairs.detail: Describe the action the control performs rather than the drawing.

pairs.label: Quarterly revenue chart
pairs.detail: Identify the visual briefly and supply equivalent structured information or a long description.

variants.hint: Ask what the image is doing on the page, not what it depicts.
variants.explanation: The correct alternative text follows the image's purpose in context, so the same pixels can require different text on different pages.

variants.title: Route by image function
variants.context: W3C guidance makes the text alternative depend on the image's purpose. Informative images convey the essential content, decorative images take empty alternative text, functional images describe the action, and complex images need a short identification plus equivalent structured information.
variants.prompt: A review finds four captions that are wrong for their route. Match each caption to the rule it breaks.

pairs.label: A blue gradient banner behind a heading receives a twelve word scene description
pairs.detail: Decorative: this image should carry empty alternative text.

pairs.label: A search button is described as a hand lens on a white circle
pairs.detail: Functional: the description must name the action, not the icon art.

pairs.label: A revenue chart receives one sentence and no data equivalent
pairs.detail: Complex: a short identification still owes an equivalent long description.

pairs.label: A product photo repeats the sentence already printed beside it
pairs.detail: Informative: do not repeat text the screen reader already announces.

variants.hint: Each caption is fluent; the mismatch is with the image's job.
variants.explanation: Fluent text that ignores image function adds noise or removes information, which is why route policy comes before wording.

variants.title: Route by image function
variants.context: W3C guidance makes the text alternative depend on the image's purpose. Informative images convey the essential content, decorative images take empty alternative text, functional images describe the action, and complex images need a short identification plus equivalent structured information.
variants.prompt: Four new uploads arrive. Match each upload to the route it belongs in.

pairs.label: A photograph of a damaged package attached to a claim form
pairs.detail: Informative image: describe the essential visible detail the claim relies on.

pairs.label: A team photo that links to the about page
pairs.detail: Functional image: describe the destination or action of the link.

pairs.label: A one pixel spacer between two sections
pairs.detail: Decorative image: empty alternative text, no description.

pairs.label: A workflow diagram with eight labeled steps
pairs.detail: Complex image: brief identification plus a structured equivalent.

variants.hint: Two of these are pictures of people or objects, but only one is informative.
variants.explanation: Routing happens before generation, because the route decides what the caption must accomplish and what it must not say.
